extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, journalism students, reporters, and writing instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive criteria for the organization, style, and comprehensibility of news stories (contrast with chronological narratives); addresses structural conventions, sentence/paragraph practices, connectives, and human-interest techniques in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Inverted Pyramid (lead + descending importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news story structure called the inverted pyramid: a summary lead followed by details arranged in descending order of importance (most important facts right after the lead; least important facts at the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to permit easy editing (cutting from the bottom) and to serve readers who skim. Criticisms: can distort chronology and causal sequence, produce incoherence, 'twist events out of their natural time sequence', and encourage emphasis on result rather than what led to it. Textbook formulations (lead; material that explains/amplifies; necessary background; secondary material) emphasize decreasing importance as the primary criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block Paragraphing (deletable independent paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that each paragraph must stand as an independent unit, deletable from the story without affecting the overall sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes editor convenience and ease of deletion but eliminates transitions and explicit anaphoric connections, thereby increasing the reader's inferencing burden and reducing coherence. Paragraphs written to be deletable cannot contain temporal or logical connectives that relate them to preceding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Sentences (keep sentences brief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic instruction to use short sentences (Flesch/Gunning guidance: under ~17 words per sentence recommended) to increase readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieved by splitting complex sentences and omitting connectives; reduces average words per sentence and is intended to make copy easier to read and faster to write under deadline. Anti-pattern: omission of connectives increases demands on the reader to infer relations; avoiding semicolons (another textbook recommendation) removes a clue that sentences are related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Paragraphs (bright, skimmable layout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraged practice of breaking text into short paragraphs for visual attractiveness and to produce extra white space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes stories visually inviting and easier to cut, but by separating related sentences into different paragraphs (without connectives) it signals non-relevance and harms the reader's ability to integrate information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing sentence and paragraph length as a newswriting sub-goal
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit subsidiary goal of newswriting: minimize sentence and paragraph length to conform to formulas and meet deadline/editing needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pressure leads writers to favor formulas, short sentences, and short paragraphs—practices that can conflict with logical organization and comprehensibility. Consider trade-offs between editor convenience/readability and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Connectives / Explicit Transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Connectives (then, because, but, as a result, in particular, earlier, later, subsequently, accordingly, therefore, thus, etc.) make the relevance of one fact to another explicit and help readers follow temporal and logical relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AP account studied had fewer connectives than fabricated narratives, increasing inferencing demands. Textbooks recognize transitional needs for inverted-pyramid stories but often propose inadequate solutions. Prefer explicit logical/temporal/spatial connectives when needed; avoid relying solely on vague or additive connectives (and, also, in addition) that provide no relation information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of rhetorical 'connective' prescriptions (repetition/pronominalization/sentence-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common textbook advice to repeat key words, use pronouns, synonyms, or repeat sentence patterns as devices to 'tie the story together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices can give the appearance of connection but do not create genuine coherence; they are symptoms rather than causes. Examples and counter-examples show that repetition/pronominalization can exist in texts that are still incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant and redundant details
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include details that are irrelevant to reasonable interpretations of the event (e.g., the color of a scarf) or redundant repetitions that add no new information (e.g., quoting sign wording that repeats the lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such details are often included to create verisimilitude or imply eyewitness status, but they clutter stories and can distract readers from the news point. Evaluate whether a detail serves interpretive or evidentiary function before including it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest elements (use with care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of anecdotes, quotations, 'personal words' and 'personal sentences' close to the lead to dramatize and spotlight the theme of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While these increase perceived interest and verisimilitude, their indiscriminate use (or placement for 'brightness') can draw attention away from the story's point and introduce irrelevant detail. Flesch-based measures (personal words per 100 words; percentage of personal sentences) quantify this tendency but do not guarantee substantive contribution to coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter objectivity and attribution constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic ethic that the reporter should not interpret or evaluate the news; stories are presented as facts for the reader to draw conclusions (the 'standard news story has no conclusion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This norm limits the reporter's use of interpretive connectives and encourages attribution of statements to sources. However, the article notes that some logical connectives (accordingly, thus, therefore) are taught yet used rarely; attribution can be invoked to avoid making necessary explicit connections—evaluate if attribution is being used to avoid clarifying relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor convenience / ease of editing as a structural driver
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of news stories (e.g., inverted pyramid, block paragraphing) is heavily influenced by the need for quick, efficient editing—stories must be easily shortened by deleting bottom paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functional constraint often takes precedence over reader comprehension and encourages designs (decreasing importance ordering, deletable blocks) that reduce explicit connective material and chronological clarity. Consider whether editorial needs are outweighing communicative clarity in a given story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative style metrics for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurable statistics used to compare writing styles: connectives per sentence, connectives per verb, total words, average words per sentence, range of words per sentence, personal words per 100 words, percentage of personal sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provide objective means to compare genres or accounts (e.g., AP vs. academic narratives) and to assess tendencies toward short sentences, sparse connectives, or human-interest load. Use them to diagnose stylistic differences but interpret in light of coherence and comprehension outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and clue-providing devices (semicolons etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation choices such as using or avoiding semicolons affect the reader's ability to see relations between sentences (a semicolon implies a close relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stylebooks urge avoiding semicolons to keep sentences short, but eliminating them removes a clue that adjacent sentences are related; balance readability prescriptions with preserving signals of cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer logical organization and explicit relevance over 'readability' tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional priority should be to emphasize comprehensibility and logical organization (making relevance explicit) rather than focusing primarily on short sentences, human-interest 'brightness', or editor convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues newswriting could be made more like other expository genres without losing objectivity or timeliness; focus teaching and evaluation on whether an account is a 'logically structured account' and whether sentence-level choices make clear the relevance of information.
